questions.q: Why does a feather fall more slowly than a rock on Earth?
choices: Rocks are pushed by the wind
Air resistance slows the feather more
questions.fact: In a vacuum, a feather and a rock fall at exactly the same speed.

questions.q: What is the pulling force in a stretched rope or string called?
questions.fact: Tug-of-war is a battle of tension in a rope.

questions.q: What does a lens that is thicker in the middle do to light?
questions.fact: Magnifying glasses use this kind of lens, called a convex lens.

questions.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?
choices: Light travels much faster than sound
Your eyes are closer to the storm
questions.fact: Counting the seconds between them and dividing by 3 gives the distance in kilometers.

questions.q: What causes thunder?
choices: Air heated by lightning expanding very fast
questions.fact: Lightning can heat the air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, hotter than the Sun's surface.

questions.q: What do we call heat moving through a solid, like a metal spoon in hot soup?
questions.fact: Metals are good conductors of heat, which is why pot handles are often made of plastic or wood.

questions.q: What do we call heat moving by warm liquid or gas rising and cool sinking?
questions.fact: Convection is why the upstairs of a house is often warmer than the downstairs.

questions.q: How does heat from the Sun reach Earth through empty space?
questions.fact: Radiation can travel through a vacuum because it does not need any material.

questions.q: What color clothing keeps you coolest in strong sunshine?
questions.fact: White reflects most light, while black absorbs it and gets warm.

questions.q: What does a thermos bottle use to keep drinks hot or cold?
questions.fact: Without air in between, heat cannot easily move by conduction or convection.

questions.q: What makes a rainbow appear in the sky?
choices: Sunlight bending and reflecting in raindrops
questions.fact: To see a rainbow, the Sun must be behind you.

questions.q: What is the word for how high or low a sound is?
questions.fact: Short, tight guitar strings make higher pitches.

questions.q: What is sound?
questions.fact: When you talk, your vocal cords vibrate and shake the air.

questions.q: What part of a guitar vibrates to make sound?
questions.fact: The hollow body makes the sound louder.

questions.q: What does a laser make?
choices: A narrow, powerful beam of light
questions.fact: The word laser started as an abbreviation of light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered radioactivity in uranium in 1896?
questions.fact: He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie.

questions.q: Which two elements did Marie and Pierre Curie discover?
questions.fact: Marie named polonium after her home country, Poland.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus?
questions.fact: Rutherford shot tiny particles at gold foil and some bounced right back.

questions.q: Which scientist proposed in the early 1800s that all matter is made of atoms?
questions.fact: The idea of atoms goes back to ancient Greece, but Dalton turned it into modern science.

questions.q: Who is often called the father of modern chemistry?
questions.fact: Lavoisier showed that burning needs oxygen and helped name it.

questions.q: Who invented the light bulb that became popular in homes in 1879?
questions.fact: Other inventors made earlier bulbs, but Edison's team made one that lasted long and was practical.

questions.q: Who discovered that white light is made of all the colors?
questions.fact: Newton passed sunlight through a prism and then recombined the colors back into white light.

questions.q: Which famous scientist was born in Germany and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
questions.fact: Einstein won it for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for relativity.

questions.q: Which scientist wrote the book Silent Spring about the dangers of pesticides?
questions.fact: The book helped start the modern environmental movement.

questions.q: Which scientist and inventor was known as the Wizard of Menlo Park?
questions.fact: Edison's lab in Menlo Park, New Jersey, was one of the first research labs.

questions.q: Which scientist is famous for his work with peanuts and helping farmers rotate crops?
questions.fact: Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts and sweet potatoes.

questions.q: What award, started by a Swedish inventor of dynamite, honors great scientists?
questions.fact: Alfred Nobel left his fortune to create the prizes, first given in 1901.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: Marie Curie won in 1903 for physics and again in 1911 for chemistry.

questions.q: What is the opposite of a vacuum, where air is squeezed tightly together?
questions.fact: Car tires hold air at high pressure to support the car's weight.

questions.q: What happens to the air pressure as you climb a tall mountain?
questions.fact: That is why your ears pop on mountain roads and airplanes.

questions.q: Why does a sealed bag of chips puff up when you take it up a mountain?
choices: The air pressure outside is lower
questions.fact: The air inside the bag pushes out harder than the thinner air outside.

questions.q: What is the name for how much water vapor is in the air?
questions.fact: High humidity makes hot days feel even hotter because sweat evaporates slowly.

questions.q: What is the scientific word for the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas?
questions.fact: Each pure substance has its own boiling point.

questions.q: Why do people put salt on icy roads?
choices: Salt soaks up all the water
Salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes
questions.fact: Salt water must get colder than fresh water to freeze.

questions.q: What happens to most materials when they are heated?
questions.fact: Bridges have gaps called expansion joints so they can grow in summer heat.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.fact: In a chemical change, new substances are made that were not there before.

questions.q: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.fact: In a physical change, the substance stays the same, it just changes form.

questions.q: What gas do we need for fire to burn?
questions.fact: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, called the fire triangle.

questions.q: Why do some fire extinguishers use carbon dioxide?
choices: It pushes away the oxygen a fire needs
questions.fact: Covering a small pan fire with a lid works the same way, by cutting off oxygen.

questions.q: What gives fireworks their bright colors?
questions.fact: Strontium makes red, copper makes blue, and barium makes green.

questions.q: Which element do all living things contain, making life carbon-based?
questions.fact: Carbon atoms can link together in chains and rings, making millions of different molecules.

questions.q: What is the most common element in the human body by mass?
questions.fact: Your body is mostly water, and oxygen makes up most of water's mass.

questions.q: What is the most common element in the universe?
questions.fact: About three quarters of all normal matter in the universe is hydrogen.

questions.q: Which shiny metal never rusts or tarnishes and is often used in jewelry?
questions.fact: Gold is so stretchy that one gram can be pulled into a wire more than 2 kilometers long.

questions.q: What is an alloy?
choices: A mix of a metal with other elements
questions.fact: Steel is an alloy made mostly of iron and a little carbon.

questions.q: Which alloy is made from copper and tin?
questions.fact: Bronze was so important that a whole period of human history is called the Bronze Age.

questions.q: Which alloy is made from copper and zinc?
questions.fact: Many trumpets and trombones are made of brass.

questions.q: Which metal is added to steel to make stainless steel that resists rust?
questions.fact: The chromium forms a thin invisible layer that protects the steel.

questions.q: What are plastics mostly made from?
questions.fact: Most plastics take hundreds of years to break down.

questions.q: What is glass mostly made from?
questions.fact: Sand is heated to over 1,500 degrees Celsius to melt it into glass.

questions.q: Which natural material comes from the sap of rubber trees?
questions.fact: Latex is made into natural rubber for things like balloons and gloves.

questions.q: What is the name of the strong, stretchy material invented in 1935 and used for stockings and ropes?
questions.fact: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fiber to become a big success.

questions.q: What is the name for tiny pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters?
questions.fact: Microplastics have been found from the deep ocean to mountaintops.

questions.q: What is a magnet strongest at?
questions.fact: You can see this by sprinkling iron filings around a bar magnet.

questions.q: Which metal is NOT attracted to a magnet?
questions.fact: That is why magnets do not stick to soda cans.

questions.q: What is a lodestone?
questions.fact: People used lodestones to make the first compasses.

questions.q: What simple viewer uses a tiny hole to safely project the Sun's image onto paper?
questions.fact: A pinhole projector lets you see the Sun's image on a piece of paper.

questions.q: What does a periscope use to let you see over things?
questions.fact: Submarines used periscopes to look above the water while staying hidden.

questions.q: What is the name for the study of sound?
questions.fact: Concert halls are carefully designed using acoustics.

questions.q: What is the study of light called?
questions.fact: Glasses, cameras and microscopes all depend on optics.

questions.q: What is the study of heat and energy called?
questions.fact: Thermo comes from the Greek word for heat.

questions.q: What is the study of how air moves around objects, like airplane wings?
questions.fact: Race cars use aerodynamics to stay pressed down onto the track.

questions.q: What helps an airplane wing create lift?
choices: Its shape makes air push it upward
questions.fact: The wing's shape and tilt turn the passing air downward, and the air pushes the wing up in return.

questions.q: What do hydraulic machines, like car brakes and diggers, use to work?
questions.fact: Liquids are hard to squeeze, so they pass a push along very well.

questions.q: What is a chemical reaction that gives off heat called?
questions.fact: Burning wood and hand warmers are exothermic reactions.

questions.q: What is a chemical reaction that takes in heat and feels cold called?
questions.fact: Instant cold packs use endothermic reactions.

questions.q: What is burning called in science?
questions.fact: Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and heat.

questions.q: What is the gas that makes soda fizzy?
questions.fact: Soda is bottled under pressure to keep the carbon dioxide dissolved.

questions.q: What is the name for the earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground?
questions.fact: Part of the smell comes from a chemical made by bacteria in soil.

questions.q: What do we call substances made of two or more elements chemically joined?
questions.fact: Water and table salt are both compounds.

questions.q: What do you call particles in water that make it cloudy and settle over time?
questions.fact: Muddy water is a suspension, so the mud slowly sinks to the bottom.

questions.q: How do you separate salt from salt water?
questions.fact: When the water evaporates, the salt crystals are left behind.

questions.q: What can you use to separate iron filings from sand?
questions.fact: The magnet pulls the iron and leaves the sand behind.

questions.q: Which way of separating mixtures uses paper to separate colors in ink?
questions.fact: Black marker ink often splits into several colors in chromatography.

questions.q: What is the process of boiling a liquid and collecting the cooled vapor called?
questions.fact: Distillation can turn salty seawater into fresh drinking water.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of an element that still has its properties?
questions.fact: It would take hundreds of thousands of atoms lined up in a row to cross the width of a human hair.

questions.q: Which particles make up protons and neutrons?
questions.fact: The name quark came from a line in a novel by James Joyce.

questions.q: What are tiny packets of light energy called?
questions.fact: Photons have no mass and always travel at the speed of light.

questions.q: What is the name of the huge particle accelerator under the border of France and Switzerland?
questions.fact: Its main ring is about 27 kilometers around.

questions.q: Which particle, sometimes called the God particle, was found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012?
questions.fact: Peter Higgs predicted it back in 1964 and won a Nobel Prize in 2013.

questions.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive substance?
choices: The time for half of it to decay
questions.fact: Carbon-14's half-life of about 5,730 years helps scientists date ancient things.

questions.q: How do scientists find the age of old bones and wood from living things?
questions.fact: Carbon dating works for things up to about 50,000 years old.

questions.q: What is the device that turns movement into electricity, used in power plants?
questions.fact: A motor does the opposite, turning electricity into movement.

questions.q: What device changes electricity into motion in things like fans and toys?
questions.fact: Electric motors work using magnets and coils of wire.

questions.q: What safety device in a home breaks a circuit when too much current flows?
questions.fact: Older homes used fuses, which melt to break the circuit.

questions.q: Why should you never touch electrical outlets with wet hands?
choices: Water helps electricity flow into your body
questions.fact: Pure water does not conduct well, but tap water has dissolved minerals that do.

questions.q: What does a solar cell turn sunlight into?
questions.fact: Solar cells are mostly made from silicon.

questions.q: What does a wind turbine turn into electricity?
questions.fact: Some wind turbine blades are more than 100 meters long.

questions.q: What is the energy that comes from the rise and fall of the ocean called?
questions.fact: Tidal energy is very predictable because tides follow the Moon.

questions.q: What are the three main fossil fuels?
questions.fact: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the air.

questions.q: What is the main gas in natural gas?
questions.fact: Gas companies add a smelly chemical so people can notice leaks, because methane has no smell.

questions.q: What kind of energy does a stretched rubber band store?
questions.fact: When you let go, the stored energy turns into motion.

questions.q: What is a perpetual motion machine?
choices: An impossible machine that would run forever without energy
questions.fact: It breaks the laws of physics because some energy is always lost as heat.

questions.q: What is the scientific study of weather called?
questions.fact: Meteorologists use satellites, balloons and computers to forecast weather.

questions.q: What do we call the temperature at which a solid melts?
questions.fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and fixed volume?
questions.fact: The particles in a solid are packed tightly and only vibrate in place.

questions.q: Which state of matter has no fixed shape but a fixed volume?
questions.fact: A liquid takes the shape of whatever container it is in.

questions.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
questions.fact: Gas particles move fast and spread far apart.

questions.q: What is a non-Newtonian fluid, like cornstarch mixed with water?
choices: A gas that turns to ice
A liquid that acts like a solid when squeezed fast
questions.fact: You can punch a pool of cornstarch slime and it feels hard, but your hand sinks if you push slowly.

questions.q: What makes a boomerang come back?
choices: The shape of its spinning wings
questions.fact: A boomerang's arms work like spinning airplane wings that make it turn.

questions.q: Which force keeps you from flying off a spinning merry-go-round?
questions.fact: Without that inward pull, you would move off in a straight line.

questions.q: What is the name for the curved path of a thrown ball?
questions.fact: Gravity pulls the ball down as it moves forward, curving its path.

questions.q: What is inertia?
choices: An object's resistance to changing its motion
questions.fact: Seat belts protect you because inertia keeps your body moving when a car stops suddenly.

questions.q: What is momentum?
questions.fact: A slow, heavy truck can have more momentum than a fast bicycle.

questions.q: What instrument measures the strength of electric current?
questions.fact: An ammeter measures current in amperes.

questions.q: Which planet's name is also the name of an element on the periodic table?
questions.fact: Uranium, neptunium and plutonium are named after planets and a dwarf planet too.

questions.q: Which element is named after Albert Einstein?
questions.fact: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of a hydrogen bomb test in 1952.

questions.q: Which element is named after Marie Curie and Pierre Curie?
questions.fact: Curium was first made in a lab in 1944.

questions.q: What tiny living thing is yeast?
questions.fact: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that people have used for baking for thousands of years.

questions.q: Why do cut apples turn brown?
choices: Chemicals in the apple react with oxygen in the air
questions.fact: Lemon juice slows the browning because its acid gets in the way of the reaction.

questions.q: Why does popcorn pop?
choices: Water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts it
questions.fact: The steam builds up pressure until the hard hull cracks open.

questions.q: What happens to the particles of a substance when it is heated?
questions.fact: Temperature is really a measure of how fast particles are moving.

questions.q: What is a crystal?
choices: A solid with atoms arranged in a repeating pattern
questions.fact: Salt and sugar grains are tiny crystals.

questions.q: What forms when water vapor freezes directly onto cold surfaces?
questions.fact: Frost forms on clear, cold nights when surfaces get colder than freezing.

questions.q: Which liquid has a higher boiling point, salt water or fresh water?
questions.fact: Dissolved salt makes water boil at a slightly higher temperature.

questions.q: What is sugar made of?
questions.fact: Table sugar's scientific name is sucrose.

questions.q: What is the main gas in the bubbles when you boil water?
questions.fact: The big bubbles in boiling water are pockets of steam.

questions.q: What happens when you mix the primary paint colors red and blue?
questions.fact: Paints mix differently from light because they absorb colors instead of giving them off.

questions.q: What color do you get by mixing red and green light?
questions.fact: This is how screens show yellow, by lighting red and green pixels together.

questions.q: What color do you see when all colors of light are mixed together?
questions.fact: White light, like sunlight, is a mix of all the colors.

questions.q: What color is an object that absorbs all colors of light?
questions.fact: Black objects get hot in the sun because they absorb so much light.

questions.q: What do you call a material that lets light pass straight through, like clear glass?
questions.fact: Wax paper is translucent, letting some light through, and wood is opaque.

questions.q: What do you call a material that blocks all light, like wood?
questions.fact: Shadows form when an opaque object blocks light.

questions.q: What happens to your shadow as the Sun gets lower in the sky?
questions.fact: Your shadow is shortest around midday, when the Sun is highest.

questions.q: Why does a spoon look bent in a glass of water?
choices: The glass is curved like a mirror
Light bends as it moves from water into air
questions.fact: This bending of light is called refraction.

questions.q: What does a concave mirror, curved inward like a spoon, do to light?
questions.fact: Car headlights and big telescopes use curved mirrors.

questions.q: Why do you see yourself upside down in the bowl of a shiny spoon?
choices: The curved surface flips the reflection
It is a trick of the metal
questions.fact: On the back of the spoon, the curve bulges out and your reflection is right side up.

questions.q: What tool can show the parts of an onion skin cell?
questions.fact: Iodine stain is often added to make the cell parts easier to see.

questions.q: What is the jelly-like fluid that fills a cell called?
questions.fact: Many of the cell's chemical reactions happen in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: What is the thin outer layer that controls what enters and leaves an animal cell?
questions.fact: The membrane lets some things in and keeps others out.

questions.q: What large storage sac holds water in plant cells?
questions.fact: When a plant's vacuoles lose water, the plant wilts.

questions.q: What is the process where one cell splits into two cells called?
questions.fact: Your body makes millions of new cells every second through cell division.

questions.q: What do we call living things made of only one cell?
questions.fact: Amoebas and most bacteria are unicellular.

questions.q: Which tiny water creature moves by changing its shape and stretching out false feet?
questions.fact: The amoeba's false feet are called pseudopods.

questions.q: What do we call a group of similar cells working together, like muscle?
questions.fact: Tissues group together to make organs.

questions.q: Which are the four groups of molecules that build all living things?
choices: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins and nucleic acids
questions.fact: Nucleic acids include DNA and RNA.

questions.q: What does a seed need to start growing?
questions.fact: Most seeds do not need light to germinate, but the young plant soon needs light to grow.

questions.q: What do roots, stems and leaves of a plant have inside to carry water?
questions.fact: Another set of tubes, called phloem, carries sugar made in the leaves.

questions.q: What is the female part of a flower that receives pollen?
questions.fact: The sticky top of the pistil, called the stigma, catches pollen grains.

questions.q: What do flowers turn into after pollination?
questions.fact: Anything with seeds inside, like a tomato or a pumpkin, is a fruit to a scientist.

questions.q: Why do sunflowers turn to face the Sun when they are young?
questions.fact: Grown-up sunflowers usually stop moving and face east.

questions.q: What is a plant's growth toward light called?
questions.fact: Houseplants on a windowsill often lean toward the window.

questions.q: Which part of a plant holds it up and carries water to the leaves?
questions.fact: Tree trunks are big, woody stems.

questions.q: Which plants reproduce with spores instead of seeds?
questions.fact: Look under a fern's leaves for brown spots, which hold the spores.

questions.q: What do plants need from soil besides water?
questions.fact: Fertilizers add minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to soil.

questions.q: What are the long-lasting traces of a living thing preserved in rock studied in science called?
questions.fact: Most fossils form when a living thing is buried quickly in mud or sand.

questions.q: What do we call a change in a gene that can create a new trait?
questions.fact: Most mutations are tiny and have no effect, but some lead to new features over many generations.

questions.q: What is it called when a living thing has a body part or behavior that helps it survive?
questions.fact: A polar bear's thick fur is an adaptation to the cold.

questions.q: What is a clone?
choices: A living thing with the exact same DNA as another
questions.fact: Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

questions.q: What is the name of the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, born in 1996?
questions.fact: Dolly was named after the singer Dolly Parton.

questions.q: What do we call the study of how traits are passed from parents to children?
questions.fact: Traits like dimples and freckles can run in families.

questions.q: What do we call germs that cause disease?
questions.fact: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites can all be pathogens.

questions.q: Why should you wash your hands with soap?
choices: Soap breaks up oils and lifts germs away
questions.fact: Scrubbing for at least 20 seconds helps remove germs.

questions.q: What is the tiny eight-legged creature that lives in pillows and eats dead skin flakes?
questions.fact: Dust mites are too small to see without a microscope.

questions.q: What do we call bacteria that live in your gut and help you digest food?
questions.fact: Your gut is home to trillions of microbes.

questions.q: Which organism glows in some ocean waves at night, making the water sparkle blue?
questions.fact: When waves stir them, these tiny organisms flash blue light.

questions.q: What is bioluminescence?
questions.fact: Fireflies, anglerfish and some mushrooms are bioluminescent.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies the chemicals in living things?
questions.fact: Biochemists helped discover how medicines work inside the body.

questions.q: What does a seismograph measure?
questions.fact: It draws wiggly lines that show how strong the shaking was.

questions.q: What is a hypothesis called once it has been tested many times and explains lots of facts?
questions.fact: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation, not just a hunch.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a renewable resource?
questions.fact: Coal takes millions of years to form, so we use it much faster than nature can replace it.

questions.q: What does recycling aluminum cans save compared with making new aluminum?
questions.fact: A recycled can can be back on a store shelf in about two months.

questions.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
choices: Plants growing faster in glass houses
Gases in the air trapping heat near Earth's surface
questions.fact: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth would be too cold for most life.

questions.q: Which gas from burning fuels is the main cause of recent global warming?
questions.fact: As of 2025, carbon dioxide levels in the air are higher than at any time in human history.

questions.q: Which gas, produced by cows burping, is a strong greenhouse gas?
questions.fact: Methane traps much more heat than carbon dioxide, though it stays in the air for less time.

questions.q: Which scientist suggested that heavier objects do not fall faster than lighter ones, against what Aristotle taught?
questions.fact: Aristotle had taught that heavy objects fall faster, and people believed it for nearly 2,000 years.

questions.q: Who explained in a 1687 book that the gravity that makes apples fall also keeps the Moon in orbit?
questions.fact: The book is often called the Principia.

questions.q: Whose improvements to the steam engine helped power the Industrial Revolution?
questions.fact: The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

questions.q: Which inventor sent the first radio signals across the Atlantic Ocean in 1901?
questions.fact: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: Who invented the code of dots and dashes used to send telegraph messages?
questions.fact: In Morse code, SOS is three dots, three dashes and three dots.

questions.q: Who invented dynamite in 1867?
questions.fact: Nobel used his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes.

questions.q: Which scientist came up with a famous thought experiment about a cat in a box?
questions.fact: The thought experiment was meant to show how strange quantum physics seems.

questions.q: What branch of physics studies the behavior of super tiny things like atoms and electrons?
questions.fact: In quantum physics, particles can act like waves.

questions.q: What is the name for a scientist's careful record of what they see during an experiment?
questions.fact: Good scientists write down everything, even results they did not expect.

questions.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments?
choices: To make sure the results are reliable
questions.fact: If others can repeat an experiment and get the same result, it is much more trustworthy.

questions.q: What do we call the amount of space something takes up?
questions.fact: You can find the volume of an odd-shaped rock by seeing how much water it pushes up in a measuring cup.

questions.q: What does a kilogram measure?
questions.fact: Since 2019, the kilogram has been defined using a number from physics instead of a metal cylinder kept in France.

questions.q: What is the metric prefix that means one thousand, as in kilometer?
questions.fact: Milli means one thousandth, so a millimeter is a thousandth of a meter.

questions.q: Which metric prefix means one millionth?
questions.fact: A micrometer is a millionth of a meter, about the size of some bacteria.

questions.q: What is the name of the tiny unit used to measure atoms and very small things, a billionth of a meter?
questions.fact: Your fingernails grow about one nanometer every second.

questions.q: Which element is a soft metal that explodes when dropped in water?
questions.fact: Sodium is stored under oil to keep it away from water and air.

questions.q: Which gas is lighter than helium but very flammable?
questions.fact: The airship Hindenburg was filled with hydrogen and burned in 1937.

questions.q: What gas did early airships like the Hindenburg use to float?
questions.fact: Modern blimps use helium instead, because it does not burn.

questions.q: Which element is a yellow solid that smells like rotten eggs when it burns or reacts?
questions.fact: Rotten eggs smell because they give off a gas made of sulfur and hydrogen.

questions.q: Which element glows in the dark and was discovered in urine in 1669?
questions.fact: Hennig Brand found it while trying to make gold.

questions.q: Which radioactive element is used as fuel in most nuclear power plants?
questions.fact: A small pellet of uranium fuel can make as much energy as about a ton of coal.

questions.q: Which element is added to toothpaste to help prevent tooth decay?
questions.fact: It is added as fluoride, which makes tooth enamel stronger.

questions.q: Which element is used in many rechargeable batteries in phones and laptops?
questions.fact: Lithium is the lightest metal of all.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest naturally common element of these?
questions.fact: Uranium has 92 protons in each atom.

questions.q: What is the densest naturally occurring element?
questions.fact: A small ball of osmium is about twice as heavy as the same size ball of lead.

questions.q: How do scientists name new elements?
choices: After the year they were found
After places, scientists, myths or properties
questions.fact: The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry approves the names.

questions.q: What are the gases in the far right column of the periodic table called?
questions.fact: Noble gases hardly react with anything.

questions.q: What are the very reactive metals in the first column of the periodic table called?
questions.fact: The farther down the column you go, the more violently they react with water.
